 1              III.    DISMANTLING COST STUDY METHODOLOGY
 2   Q.   Please describe the Dismantling Study prepared for SPS.

 3   A.   SPS retained BMcD to provide a recommendation regarding the total cost, in 2024

 4        dollars, for dismantling each generation unit and the common facilities at each of

 5        the generating plants at the end of the useful life of each facility, net of salvage

 6        value for scrap materials at each plant. Our estimates are inclusive of direct costs

 7        associated with decommissioning and demolishing the plant equipment and

 8        facilities and restoring the sites to an industrial condition. The direct costs include

 9        environmental remediation costs for asbestos removal and other hazardous material

10        handling and disposal, as well as costs for closing any ponds and cleaning up

11        potentially contaminated soil.

12   Q.   What was the extent of your personal involvement in the preparation of the

13        Dismantling Study?

14   A.   I served as the BMcD Managing Director on the Dismantling Study. I worked

15        directly with all individuals and parties involved in the preparation of the

16        dismantling cost estimates in the Dismantling Study. I was responsible for the

17        overall project and was involved in the development of the decommissioning and

18        dismantling    assumptions,      decommissioning     and    dismantling    estimating

19        methodology, preparation and review of the estimates, and preparation and review

20        of the report. In addition, BMcD representatives and engineers visited each

21        generation unit (excluding Cunningham 1 Solar, Cunningham 1 Battery Energy

2        facilities had not yet been constructed at the time the Study was prepared) to

3        perform a tour of each facility with plant personnel to review the equipment, and I

4        relied on information obtained during those tours in my analyses.

 3   Q.   Were all Plants in service at the time the Dismantling Study was prepared?

 5        for the Cunningham 1 BESS, Cunningham 1 Solar, Cunningham 2 Solar, and Plant

 6        X Solar facilities, which had not yet been constructed at the time of the Study.

 7   Q.   Is it common that dismantling studies are performed for solar and battery

 8        projects that have not yet reached commercial operation?

 9   A.   Yes, dismantling studies are commonly performed for solar and battery projects

10        prior to a facility reaching commercial operation. For instance, as part of the

11        bonding process and permitting process for zoning solar and battery projects, a

12        dismantling study is typically required. Also, many counties require financial

13        assurance to be in place in advance of construction for the decommissioning and

14        dismantling of the project in the event the project becomes a stranded asset. In

15        these cases, battery and solar project dismantling estimates are prepared based on

16        review of drawings and other relevant documentation without a site visit, since at

17        this stage none of the project equipment is in place.

18               Although the Cunningham 1 BESS, Cunningham 1 Solar, Cunningham 2

19        Solar, and Plant X Solar facilities were not in commercial operation at the time of

20        the Dismantling Study, my team and I were able to rely on construction drawings,

 1        including site plans, floor plans, foundation drawings, equipment locations and

 2        types, and transmission line documentation to prepare the Study and recommend a

 3        dismantling cost for these facilities, which is information commonly relied on when

 4        performing dismantling studies prior to a facility entering commercial operation.

 5   Q.   Explain the type of costs reflected in a dismantling study.

 6   A.   Dismantling study cost estimates generally include both direct and indirect costs

 7        associated with decommissioning, demolishing equipment and facilities, and

 8        restoring the site to an appropriate condition. For thermal units, the estimates

 9        assume restoration to an industrial condition. Direct costs include environmental

10        remediation—such as asbestos removal, hazardous materials handling, and

11        contaminated soil disposal.

12               For wind and solar units, the estimates assume restoration to an

13        agricultural condition, consistent with surrounding use. These facilities are usually

14        located on leased agricultural land, so returning the site to pre-construction use

15        (e.g., farming or grazing) is standard. Direct costs include remediation for oil,

16        chemicals, and other hazardous materials. In addition to these direct costs,

17        dismantling studies also include estimates of indirect costs incurred during

18        decommissioning, as well as contingency costs, which I address in the next section

19        of my testimony.

1    Q.   What does restoring the site for industrial use require?

2    A.   Each site will have all above-grade buildings and equipment removed, have

3         foundations removed to four feet below grade, be rough graded, and seeded. The

4         sites also will have underground piping 24 inches and larger filled with flowable

5         concrete fill or grout and capped. Ponds will have liners removed and be graded to

6         match surrounding areas. Since the future use of each site is unknown, restoring

7         each site to the standard of industrial use allows SPS flexibility regarding the

8         potential future use. The sites can alternately remain in this condition in perpetuity.

9    Q.   Why is it reasonable to restore the fossil fuel sites to the standard for industrial

10        use?

11   A.   It is reasonable to assume the sites of the fossil units would be restored to the

12        standard of industrial use as this is a common practice, removes liabilities, and

13        avoids future carrying costs associated with maintaining or insuring the remaining

14        facilities that could at some point exceed the cost of demolition, while maintaining

15        flexibility of future site use. For example, restoring the site in this manner enables

16        the site to be reused for another power plant, to be redeveloped for industrial use,

17        or to be sold for similar uses.

18   Q.   What types of liabilities and carrying costs are you referring to?

19   A.   These costs would include, but not be limited to, items such as liability insurance

20        and property taxes, site security, structural inspections of stacks, and maintaining

 1        environmental permits. All of these costs would be necessary to maintain a safe

 2        site and be in compliance with applicable regulations.

 3   Q.   What approach was used to develop the direct cost estimates in the

 4        Dismantling Study?

 5   A.   As mentioned above, the dismantling cost estimates were developed based on

 6        estimates of direct costs, indirect costs, and contingency. The direct dismantling

 7        cost estimates were based on what I would expect an outside contractor, selected

 8        through a competitive bidding process, to charge SPS to demolish the site,

 9        dismantle all equipment, address environmental issues, and restore the site to a

10        condition suitable for industrial use, based on performing known decommissioning

11        and dismantling tasks within the set of assumptions outlined in the Dismantling

12        Study and under ideal conditions.         Site-specific direct cost estimates were

13        developed using a “bottom-up” cost estimating approach, where cost estimates are

14        developed from scratch through the development of site-specific quantity estimates

15        and the application of unit pricing to the quantity estimates. The quantity estimates

16        include but are not limited to items such as tons of steel; pounds of other metals

17        such as copper and stainless steel; tons of debris; cubic yards of concrete; linear

18        feet of asbestos pipe insulation; square feet of asbestos boiler insulation; cubic

19        yards of site grading; acres of seeding; and the labor hours required to complete the

20        decommissioning and demolition activities.

 1   Q.   Where are the assumptions outlined in the Dismantling Study?

 2   A.   The assumptions applied to the cost estimates are documented in Section 4.1 of the

 3        Dismantling Study, Attachment JTK-2 to my direct testimony.

 4   Q.   How were specific quantities and unit pricing estimated for purposes of

 5        estimating site-specific direct costs?

 6   A.   The BMcD team estimated quantities based on a visual inspection of the facilities,

 7        discussions with plant staff, review of engineering drawings, our in-house database

 8        of plant quantities, and our professional judgment. Using this information, we

 9        estimated the reasonable costs for the tasks required to decommission and demolish

10        each of the subject facilities. Current market pricing for labor rates, equipment,

11        and unit pricing were then developed for each task. These rates were applied to the

12        quantities for the Plants to determine the total direct cost of dismantling each site.

13        Additionally, unit pricing for scrap values was applied to the scrap quantities to

14        determine anticipated salvage values, which are addressed later in my testimony.

15   Q.   What sources did you rely on to develop the direct cost estimates for the

16        Plants?

17   A.   The labor rates, equipment costs, and disposal costs used to develop the

18        Dismantling Study cost estimates were specific to the locations in which the work

19        was to be performed. These rates were applied to the quantities associated with each

20        Plant to determine the total cost of decommissioning and demolishing. Disposal

21        costs were obtained from publicly available information and communications with

                                       Jeffrey T. Kopp

 1        landfills and scrap processors located in the area in which the work is to be

 2        performed to result in estimates that are site-specific and account for local markets,

 3        costs and conditions.

 4               Pricing developed by the Fastmarkets was also used to develop scrap

 5        credits, as discussed in more detail in Section V of my testimony. The Fastmarkets

 6        is an industry standard publication routinely relied upon by demolition contractors.

 7        Scrap costs also included a deduction for transportation from each site to the

 8        selected scrap market in order to create estimates that are site-specific and account

 9        for local markets, costs and conditions.

10   Q.   Did you rely on any other sources?

11   A.   Yes. The RS Means online database was utilized to obtain labor rates, equipment

12        costs, and disposal costs for the study area. RS Means labor rates are national

13        averages and include site cost indices to provide localized costs to determine costs

14        that are as site-specific as possible. RS Means is widely utilized within the

15        construction industry as a tool for estimating and projecting project costs.

16   Q.   Are these sources generally accepted in the industry and relied upon by other

17        regulatory authorities in establishing dismantling costs?

18   A.   Yes. These sources are recognized industry-wide, and I have relied on them for the

19        dismantling cost estimates I have prepared for over 200 units; furthermore, my

20        recommended dismantling costs based on these sources have been approved in New

21        Mexico and other states which I have participated in regulatory proceedings.

 1   Q.   Did you utilize “craft labor” or overtime in your cost estimates?

 2   A.   No. As shown in my study, I utilized the B-8 Crew from RS Means, which is an

 3        appropriate crew for these types of activities.

 4   Q.   Did you consider whether the resale of any equipment would be feasible to

 5        offset your estimated dismantling costs?

 6   A.   Yes. I do not believe resale is feasible due to the limited and opportunistic market

 7        for equipment resale. In our recent experience with power plant retirements, it has

 8        been difficult to find buyers of used equipment willing to pay more than the scrap

 9        value of the equipment because the market for specific buyers with a need for the

10        specific equipment at the time of dismantling is typically very limited.

11        Furthermore, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, more than

12        130 gigawatts of fossil-fueled capacity has been retired in the last decade and there

13        are more than 35 gigawatts of additional announced retirements in the next five

14        years, representing closures of more than 200 additional units, so it is anticipated

15        the market would be flooded with used equipment and the potential buyers of that

16        used equipment would be even further reduced, putting downward pressure on used

17        equipment pricing. Based on these conditions, I do not think resale is feasible or

18        reasonable to presume in my cost estimates. It is reasonable to assume the expected

19        value of the equipment should be limited to its scrap value.

21        for various types of non-nuclear power generating assets. Technology-specific

 1                   IV.    INDIRECT AND CONTINGENCY COSTS
 2   Q.   What is included in the project indirect costs?

 3   A.   Indirect costs include those costs expected to be incurred by SPS during the

 4        dismantling process that are in addition to the direct costs paid to demolition

 5        contractors. This includes the internal administrative costs (e.g., permitting, fees,

 6        SPS employee allocated expense) or costs associated with third-party project

 7        managers or engineers providing oversight during demolition activities,

 8        inspections, and testing to confirm that remediation has been completed.

 9   Q.   How were the indirect costs determined?

10   A.   Indirect costs were determined as a percentage of the direct costs, as is a typical

11        approach when preparing these types of cost estimates.          We developed the

12        percentage of direct costs that was applied to determine the indirect costs based on

13        input from SPS regarding their approach to managing the execution of the

14        dismantling projects.

15   Q.   What input did you receive from SPS regarding the indirect costs?

16   A.   SPS provided input on its actual expenditures on indirect costs experienced on

17        actual demolition projects for Xcel Energy’s Colorado utility, Public Service

18        Company of Colorado. Accordingly, we based the indirect costs in the Dismantling

19        Study on Xcel Energy’s actual indirect costs experience.

 1   Q.   What is included in the contingency costs?

 2   A.   This category includes costs reasonably expected to be incurred by SPS during the

 3        execution of decommissioning and demolition activities, as discussed previously.

 4        For dismantling projects, there is uncertainty associated with work conditions and

 5        how the work will be performed. There is also some uncertainty associated with

 6        estimating the quantities for dismantlement of facilities, due to the age and limits

 7        on drawings available, and the absence of testing results for environmental

 8        contamination prior to preparation of these types of studies. Contingency costs

 9        account for these unspecified but expected costs and are in addition to the direct

10        costs associated with the base dismantling costs for known scope items.

2.0 Introduction
2.1       Background
1898 & Co. was retained by Xcel Energy to conduct a Decommissioning Cost Study for power generation and
energy storage assets located in New Mexico and Texas. The assets include natural gas-fired, coal-fired,
wind, and solar generating facilities as well as an energy storage facility. Individuals from 1898 & Co.
conducted site visits for the Plants that were built at the time of the Study. The purpose of the Study was to
review the facilities and to make a recommendation to Xcel Energy regarding the total cost to decommission
and dismantle the facilities at the end of their useful lives.

1898 & Co. has prepared over three hundred decommissioning studies on various types of fossil fuel and
renewable power plants. In addition to preparing decommissioning and dismantling cost estimates, 1898 &
Co. has supported demolition projects as the owner’s engineer. In this capacity, 1898 & Co. has evaluated
demolition bids and overseen demolition activities. This has provided 1898 & Co. with insight into a broad
range of competitive demolition bids, which also assists in confirming the validity of the decommissioning
and dismantling estimates developed by 1898 & Co.

2.2       Methodology
The decommissioning and dismantling costs were developed using information provided by Xcel Energy and
in-house data 1898 & Co. has collected from previous project experience. 1898 & Co. estimated quantities
for equipment based on a visual inspection of the facilities, reviews of engineering drawings, an in-house
database of plant equipment quantities, and professional judgement. For each Plant, quantities were
estimated for each required task. Current market pricing for labor rates and equipment was then developed
for each task. The unit pricing was developed for each site based on labor rates, equipment costs, and
disposal costs specific to the area in which the work is to be performed. These rates were applied to the
quantities for the Plants to determine the total cost of decommissioning and dismantling.

The decommissioning and dismantling costs include the cost to return each site to an industrial condition,
suitable for reuse for development of an industrial facility. Included are the costs to decommission and
dismantle all the assets owned by Xcel Energy at each site, including power generating equipment, energy
storage equipment, and BOP facilities.

4.0 Decommissioning and Dismantling Costs
1898 & Co. has prepared decommissioning and dimsantling cost estimates for the Plants. When Xcel Energy
determines that each site should be retired, the above grade equipment and steel structures are assumed to
have scrap value to a scrap contractor which will offset a portion of the site decommissioning costs.
However, Xcel Energy will incur costs of decommissioning and dismantling the Plants and restoration of the
sites to the extent that those costs exceed the scrap value of equipment and bulk steel.

The decommissioning and dismantling costs for each site include the cost to return each site to an industrial
condition, suitable for reuse for development of an industrial facility. Included are the costs to dismantle all
the assets owned by Xcel Energy at the sites, including power generating and energy storage equipment and
BOP facilities, as well as the costs to perform environmental site restoration activities.

For purposes of this study, 1898 & Co. assumed that each site will be dismantled as a single project, allowing
the most cost-effective demolition methods to be utilized. A summary of several of the means and methods
that could be employed is summarized in the following paragraphs; however, means and methods will not be
dictated to the contractor by 1898 & Co. It will be the contractor’s responsibility to determine means and
methods that result in safely dismantling the Plants at the lowest possible cost.

Asbestos remediation, as required, would take place prior to commencement of any other demolition
activities. Abatement would need to be performed in compliance with all state and federal regulations,
including, but not limited to, requirements for sealing off work areas and maintaining negative pressure
throughout the removal process. Final clearances and approvals would need to be achieved prior to
performing further demolition activities.

High grade assets would then be removed from the site to the extent possible. This would include items such
as transformers, transformer coils, circuit breakers, electrical wire, condenser plates and tubes, and heater
tubes. High grade assets include precious alloys such as copper, aluminum-brass tubes, stainless steel tubes,
and other high value metals occurring in plant systems. High grade asset removal would occur up-front in the
schedule, to reduce the potential for theft, to increase cash flow, and for separation of recyclable materials
to increase scrap recovery. Methods of removal vary with the location and nature of the asset. Small
transformers, small equipment, and wire would likely be removed and shipped as-is for processing at a scrap
yard. Large transformers, CT, ST generators, and condensers would likely require some on-site disassembly
prior to being shipped to a scrap yard.

Construction and Demolition (“C&D”) waste includes items such as non-asbestos insulation, roofing, wood,
drywall, plastics, and other non-metallic materials. C&D waste would typically be segregated from scrap and
concrete to avoid cross-contamination of waste streams or recycle streams. C&D crews could remove these
materials with equipment such as excavators equipped with material handling attachments, skid steers, etc.
This material would be consolidated and loaded into bulk containers for disposal.

In general, boilers and Heat Recovery Steam Generators (“HRSG”) could be felled and cut into manageable
sized pieces on the ground. First the structures around the boilers would need to be removed using
excavators equipped with shears and grapples. Stairs, grating, elevators, and other high structures would be
removed using an “ultra-high reach” excavator, equipped with shears. Following removal of these
structures, the boilers or HRSGs would be felled, using explosive blasts. The boilers would then be
dismantled using equipment such as excavators equipped with shears and grapples, and the scrap metal
loaded onto trailers for recycling.
